title: Plaited stitch
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), fig. 382. Public domain. Also described in Mary Thomas, Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938). Out of copyright UK/EU.

glossaryTerms.definition: The number of stitches and rows per 10 cm in a given yarn on a given needle size. Called 'gauge' in US knitting.

content.text: The secret of plaited stitch is that every stitch is worked

on every row. This permanently crosses the legs of each stitch and makes the fabric look braided or woven rather than looped. The crossed structure holds the stitches firmly together, giving a denser, firmer cloth from the same yarn and needles that would produce an open stocking stitch.

You need yarn and needles. Compare a plaited swatch to a stocking stitch swatch of the same size: the plaited version will be noticeably narrower and feel stiffer before blocking. Allow for this by going up one needle size if you want to match a stocking-stitch

content.text: Cast on any number of stitches.
Right-side row: knit every stitch through the back loop (k tbl) across.
Wrong-side row: purl every stitch through the back loop (p tbl) across.
Repeat rows 2 and 3. The right side of the fabric will show a closely packed braided surface. The wrong side will look similar but with the braid direction slightly different.

Plaited stitch appears in Victorian knitting manuals as a sturdy fabric for stocking legs, children's garments, and domestic cloths. In Eastern European and Balkan traditions it is the default stitch for garments, not a textured variation. It also appears in sock-heel panels and in dishcloths where the added density helps with scrubbing.
Unintentionally tight fabric. The combination of k tbl and p tbl tightens
more than k tbl alone. Swatch before committing to a full project: often one needle size up is needed.

Wrong-side rows slipping back to standard purl. The p tbl entry point is easy to lose track of. A stitch marker placed at the start of every wrong-side row as a reminder can help while the habit is forming.
What to try next: combine plaited stitch with a standard stocking stitch background to create textured stripe or panel effects within a garment body.
